title: Janaka's bow
hook: a priest asks about his mother, and a king tells where his bow, and his daughter, came from

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ahalya restored, part two: no stone in Valmiki, but a woman unseen, freed by being seen and by hosting her guests. Your line was seen, honored, and hosting.

The travelers reach Mithila, and King Janaka comes out to receive them with his priests. One is Shatananda, Janaka's chief priest. His first question to Vishvamitra isn't about the bow, or the princes, or the sacrifice. Did you show my mother to Rama? Was she honored? Did my father come back to her? Shatananda is Ahalya and Gautama's eldest son. Yesterday's story was his family's. And when he hears yes, she's free, they're together, he's overjoyed. Then the king speaks of something else.
screen: `MITHILA, AND ITS PRIEST.` → `DID YOU SHOW MY MOTHER TO RAMA?` → `YES. SHE'S FREE.`

segments.voice: These boys would like to see the bow, Vishvamitra says, and Janaka tells its story. Long ago, at the great sacrifice of Daksha, Shiva was refused his share of the offerings. In anger he raised this very bow against the gods, ready to cut them down. The gods begged him to relent; he did, and gave them the bow. The gods gave it to Devarata, an ancestor of Janaka's line, to keep, and it has stayed in Mithila ever since. A bow that once threatened the gods. Then Janaka tells a second story, about his daughter. Once, he says, I was plowing a field to prepare for a sacrifice, and out of the furrow the plow had cut, a girl rose up. I raised her as my own and named her Sita. Sita means furrow, the line a plow cuts. She wasn't born from a womb, the text says; she came from the earth itself. That's why she's often called Bhumija, daughter of the earth, and Janaki, daughter of Janaka. So in one speech the king sets two things side by side: a bow of Shiva, kept for generations, and a daughter of the soil, raised with love. And he's decided that only the one who can handle the first can marry the second. Tomorrow, what that has cost him.
screen: `SHATANANDA, AHALYA'S SON.` · `SHIVA'S BOW, RAISED AT DAKSHA'S RITE.` · `KEPT BY JANAKA'S LINE.` · `SITA RISES FROM THE FURROW.` · then, large: `SĪTĀ: THE FURROW.`

segments.voice: Feel the ground beneath you, the floor, the foundation, the earth under that, and let your weight sink into it, held by it and fed by it the way Sita was. Breathe in and feel the earth support you; breathe out and give your weight back to it.
Janaka's bow. The bow of Shiva, kept in Mithila since Daksha's sacrifice, and the test Janaka sets for whoever would marry Sita, the daughter of the furrow.
Your line: Sita rising from the furrow. A daughter of the earth, raised with love. That's day five hundred seven.

howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Sita's appearance from the earth on Sita Navami, in the month of Vaishakha, and Mithila, in today's Bihar and Nepal's Janakpur region, holds her as its own daughter.

original.note: Sanskrit sītā: a furrow, the line cut by a plow. Janaka's daughter, found in one.

trapdoor: what you thought: the bow is just a strength test for suitors.
what it means: it's Shiva's bow, kept for generations, and Janaka sets it beside a daughter born from the earth.
what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 66 gives the bow's history from Daksha's sacrifice to Devarata, and Sita as ayonija, not womb-born, found in the furrow while Janaka prepared ground for a rite.

chat.says: Why is Sita called a daughter of the earth?
options: Janaka found her rising from a furrow as he plowed, and raised her as his own.
She was born on the day of Mithila's big harvest festival, so the name stuck.
Her birth family were farmers, and Janaka adopted her when she was a baby.
chat.meaning: Sita means furrow. Janaka says she rose from the furrow his plow cut, so she's called Bhumija, daughter of the earth.
